A1.justification: Both PDFs describe MuLan and contain readable methods, equations, experimental results, figures, and appendices A–B. Corresponding material can be matched despite substantial reformatting and experimental reorganization.

before.justification: v1 reports original multilingual generation experiments on XM18, DPG-Bench and COCO2014, together with architecture, semantic-alignment and data-efficiency analyses.

after.justification: v2 reports original XM12 and COCO2014 evaluations, additional baseline and metric comparisons, and retained semantic-alignment and data-efficiency analyses.

M1.justification: Both versions train an English-data adapter between a frozen multilingual encoder and frozen diffusion model. MLP adapters for PixArt, learned-query transformers for Stable Diffusion, and dual transformers with pooling for SDXL already appear in v1. The revised explanation and overview diagram do not establish a new procedure.

E1.justification: v2 removes the five-language DPG-Bench instruction-following evaluation and narrows the main XM3600 comparison from 18 to 12 languages. The six omitted XM3600 languages remain represented in the retained 85-language COCO2014 evaluation. Training datasets and qualitative application coverage are retained; new metrics on XM12 do not restore the removed DPG-Bench coverage.

E2.justification: v2 adds evaluated GlueGen, NLLB-based translation pipelines for SD15 and PixArt, Google-Translate-based PixArt, and untranslated SD15/PixArt baselines in Tables 3 and 5. AltDiffusion also enters the main SD15 XM comparison, having appeared in other v1 experiments. AltDiffusion-m18/AltDiffusion and ViT-XLM-R-L/Mul-OpenCLIP are matched names, not newly introduced comparators.

E3.justification: v2 adds FID, similarity scoring with LAION's multilingual CLIP, and GPT-4o-based VQAScore, substantially extending the evaluation protocol. The text-encoder comparison is now reported as an average over five non-English languages, replacing English/Spanish/French/Chinese breakdowns. These are reported evaluation changes; they do not establish that retained experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: The MLP versus one-layer/four-layer transformer ablation in v1 Table 6 disappears. v2 adds an explicit check of dependence on the similarity evaluator and consolidates the text-encoder/alignment analyses into a revised comparison. The data-size sensitivity experiment and t-SNE analysis remain unchanged, rather than being new supplementary evidence.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, random seeds, confidence intervals, error bars or significance tests for the generation results. Across-language averages remain point summaries rather than uncertainty estimates.

E6.justification: v2 adds extensive FID, alternative-CLIP and VQAScore results while removing DPG-Bench, architecture-ablation and specialized MuLan-SDXL result entries. Its new FID comparison reports 11.8 for MuLan-PixArt versus 9.1 for AltDiffusion. Headline CLIP scores change from 38.61/37.61 to 39.57/39.61, without establishing a same-setting gain. The full COCO2014 and data-size tables are numerically unchanged.

T1.justification: Equations 1–4 and their optimization formulations are retained. Neither version supplies formal theorems or proofs, and v2's additional alignment explanations introduce no new mathematical assumptions or derivations.

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction and conclusion retain the same central contributions: efficient multilingual adaptation using aligned encoders, English-only adapter training, support for over 110 languages, and compatibility with existing diffusion tools. Updated headline scores change the reported evidence without materially redefining these claims.

C2.justification: v2 adds a hypothesis explaining image-centered alignment's advantage through prior visual grounding, discusses CLIP's limitations for compositional details, and acknowledges worse FID alongside stronger aesthetic scores. The earlier word-order explanation for transformer adapters disappears. The conclusion's limitations concerning paired-data bias, distribution shift and prompt understanding remain.

D1.justification: v2 removes the explicit 77-query setting and the CCMatrix alignment recipe specifying 2.91B samples, batch size 512, learning rate 2e-5 and ten epochs. Section 4.1 revises training-time descriptions from within two/four days to 12 hours/two days. Main adapter optimization settings remain; the timing revisions do not establish an algorithmic speedup.

R1.justification: v2 substantially sharpens positioning against closely related lightweight adapters by introducing GlueGen and PEA-Diffusion in Section 2. It distinguishes MuLan through ordinary diffusion-loss training and image-centered alignment, then develops explicit comparisons with GlueGen and AltDiffusion in Section 4.2. This revises the relationship to prior approaches beyond adding citations.

P1.justification: The experimental narrative is extensively rewritten into focused comparison paragraphs, and the former appendix PixArt and alignment discussions are incorporated into the main evaluation. Appendix A is consolidated and reordered, references move before the appendices, and an impact statement is added. Much of the introduction and conclusion remains recognizable.

P2.justification: Figure 2 is redrawn from an architecture overview with backbone-specific adapter internals into a compact integration diagram showing optional community tools. Main result tables become broad method-by-language and multi-metric matrices, with other tables removed or consolidated. The conference layout changes throughout, while retained appendix plots and galleries are relocated.

improvement.justification: The added GlueGen, translation and untranslated-input controls, together with alternative CLIP and VQAScore evaluations, better test MuLan's central effectiveness claims and reduce reliance on its own conditioning encoder for evaluation. These gains are partly offset by losing DPG-Bench coverage, the architecture ablation and CCMatrix reproducibility details. The evidence supports a limited net improvement in paper quality.
